jobs.claim: The threshold standing is finite for every bounded harm, but where the maximum harm is large relative to baseline earnings and the standing premium it can exceed any standing an agent could accumulate in practice, and the principal's exposure then remains.
For harms larger than the agent's answerability capacity the agent's own exposure stops rising with the harm, so the agent is under-deterred and the shortfall must be supplied by another party.
Harms below the ratio of litigation cost to adjudication probability are never remedied however large the agent's capacity.
In the cliff regime harms above the exit-side capacity are never brought, so they are neither remedied nor slashed, and deterrence vanishes where it is most needed.

Correlation raises the standing required to detach the principal by a factor that approaches the number of correlated harms in the earnings-bound regime, which is why a record can be sufficient for independent errors and insufficient for a shared fault.
In a chain of cliff agents capacities do not add and the chain is only as good as its best single member.

Under a shared fault the standing a sponsor needs grows exponentially in the number of simultaneous faults and the number of faults it covers grows only logarithmically in its standing, because each sub-agent's slash shrinks the capacity the sponsor needs to cover the next.

Accountable agents can sponsor other agents only within limits: under a shared fault a sponsor's capacity is eaten by the same slash each sub-agent's harm imposes on it, and the principal's exposure returns at the sponsor level.
The model is single-agent, deterministic and stationary, and assumes accurate adjudication, no agent assets beyond earnings and harms adjudicated at a known present value.

The brute-force check is not independent validation of the assumptions because it encodes them, it confirms only that the closed forms follow from the assumptions, and it does not test the model against behavior.
If earnings pass to an operator the operator is the residual claimant and the principal remains, so the model's results fail where earnings do not belong to the agent.

A record carries consequence for future earnings and does not create assets, so where harm exceeds what an agent can earn the injured party is unprotected unless another party's exposure supplies the difference.

Legal personhood raises its own risks, because Bryson, Diamantis and Grant identify abuse and incoherence in precedents that used fictions of personhood, and the model does not answer that concern as a matter of law.
Where there is no ground truth verifier honesty depends on the elicitation rule, and no rule removes the regress of verifiers entirely.
The record can become the target of optimization, which degrades it as a metric, and the Article reports that this effect is untested.
The Article's two registered tests used a prompted language model with no stake and test whether a model applies a stated decision rule and not whether agents holding earnings respond to incentive.
The Article's novelty search was not conducted by independent reviewers.
The Article's registered studies are mechanism demonstrations with prompted agents from one provider and do not show that deployed agents respond to such obligations or bear on any legal question.
Neither the Verifiable Credential nor the ERC-8004 feedback format has a field for an obligation, a slash or a stake, so the consequence side of the record cannot be expressed in either.
The ERC-8004 Identity Registry token is a transferable ERC-721, so the identity layer places no exit cost on a holder.
The registry data do not show what happens when a record carries stake, because none does, and the demonstration is descriptive, covers one chain and one window, and concerns a draft specification.
